claims.text: As-cast HfZrTiTa0.53 has a predominantly single-phase BCC microstructure.
HfZrTiTa0.53 has limited tensile ductility, represented by an approximately 13.5% terminal strain.
Warm rolling HfZrTiTa0.53 at 600–700 °C followed by annealing near 750 °C for 1–2 hours will refine its grains and substructure.
An anneal near 750 °C is sub-transus for HfZrTiTa0.53.
The proposed warm-rolling and annealing treatment will activate deformation twinning in HfZrTiTa0.53.
The treatment will produce fine grains, twin boundaries, and an enhanced dislocation network.
Fine grains, twin boundaries, and an enhanced dislocation network will delay necking during tensile deformation.
Grain refinement, deformation twinning, and increased dislocation mobility will enhance strain hardening.
Enhanced strain hardening will delay necking and improve uniform tensile elongation.
Retention of the primary phase will preserve the alloy's high yield strength.
Retention of the primary phase will preserve impact-triggered energy release.
The treatment will increase uniform tensile elongation by approximately 50–100%, to more than 20%.
After treatment, yield strength will remain near 786 MPa.
After treatment, impact-triggered energy release will remain comparable to that of the as-cast alloy.
HfZrTiTa0.53 has a baseline yield strength of about 786 MPa.
HfZrTiTa0.53 has a baseline compressive strength of 1314 MPa and terminal strain near 13.5%.
Previous measurements establish high impact-triggered energy release for HfZrTiTa0.53.
The predicted improvement applies at room temperature under quasi-static tensile loading over strain rates of 10^-3 to 10^1 s^-1.

contradictions.description: The 13.5% terminal strain is presented as evidence of limited tensile ductility and then used as the numerical baseline for uniform tensile elongation, although terminal strain, total tensile elongation, uniform tensile elongation, and compressive terminal strain are distinct metrics.

The prediction requires a 50–100% increase in uniform elongation, but the stated rule falsifies only improvements below 20%. An improvement between 20% and 50% would violate the prediction without falsifying it under the stated rule.
The full strain-rate interval from 10^-3 to 10^1 s^-1 is labeled quasi-static, although its upper end is not ordinarily treated as quasi-static tensile loading.
